--- title: "From a model to a claim" description: "A claim puts a model's numbers into words. On the survey a random forest's Methods and Results paragraphs are written from the code, the simulation confirms the temperature shape but not a depth peak, and a gear that misses animals on mud turns more animals on mud into fewer while the cross-validated score improves." order: 6 categories: [interpretation, reproducibility] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A claim puts a model's numbers into words A study ends in sentences: a Methods paragraph that says what was done and a Results paragraph that says what was found. Each sentence is a **claim**, and a reader takes the claims away, not the numbers. A good claim says what was found, how sure the finding is, and how far it reaches. This page writes both paragraphs for a random forest fitted to the survey, so that each sentence carries its evidence, and shows how to tell the sentences the survey supports from those it cannot, including one that every check inside the model would pass. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A claim passes three checks A model's score says how well it predicts the records it is given. A claim is about the species, and getting from one to the other takes three checks: - **The model beats a baseline.** Scored on sites it never saw, it predicts better than the average does. [Cross-validation](../07-validation/cross-validation.qmd) makes this check. - **The data separate the inputs.** Two inputs that move together on the survey cannot be told apart by any model. This is set by where the stations were placed. - **The records match the water.** A gear that misses some animals changes the records at every station it fishes, and the model learns the change. ::: {.diagram} ![Three checks before a claim. Cross-validation checks that the model beats a baseline on new sites. Whether the data separate two inputs depends on the survey's design, and whether the records match what was in the water is checked outside the model.](img/three-checks.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Beats a baseline, checked by cross-validation: scored on sites it never saw, against predicting the average; two bars for the error on new sites, the model's shorter than the average's. Inputs the data separate, set by the survey's design: two inputs that move together cannot be told apart by any model; a scatter of stations along a diagonal band of depth against distance offshore, with the empty corners marked no stations. Records match the water, checked outside the model: a gear that misses animals biases every fold alike; eight animals in the water on mud, four recorded. A note says cross-validation makes the first check, and the other two need knowledge of how the data were collected."} ::: ## Worked example A random forest is scored against predicting the average by ten-fold cross-validation by site. On each fold it also gives each held-out station a 90% interval, as the quantile forest of [Communicating uncertainty](communicating-uncertainty.qmd), and each input is shuffled on the held-out sites, as in [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd). The two paragraphs are written from these results and from the forest's [partial dependence](partial-effects.qmd). The survey is simulated, so the shapes are then checked against the ones the simulation used. Last, the records are biased as a gear that misses half the animals on mud would bias them, and the whole report is run again. ### Preparing the data Three columns of random numbers are added to the inputs, as in [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd), to show what an unused input scores. The folds are drawn inside a function with its own seed, as [Reproducibility and transparent reporting](reproducibility.qmd) recommends, so the biased records later get exactly the same folds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") # three columns of random numbers, unrelated to anything in the survey modelling <- survey |> select(site_id, abundance, all_of(inputs)) |> mutate(random_1 = rnorm(n()), random_2 = rnorm(n()), random_3 = rnorm(n())) # whole sites in each fold, the same folds for any version of the records site_folds <- function(data) { set.seed(123) group_vfold_cv(data, group = site_id, v = 10) } forest_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ ., data = modelling) |> update_role(site_id, new_role = "site") |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) # a quantile forest predicts like a random forest and also gives intervals forest <- workflow(forest_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 300) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123, quantreg = TRUE)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence, permutation_importance from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() # three columns of random numbers, unrelated to anything in the survey rng = np.random.default_rng(123) for i in (1, 2, 3): survey[f"random_{i}"] = rng.standard_normal(len(survey)) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "random_1", "random_2", "random_3"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical # whole sites in each fold, the same folds for any version of the records def site_folds(data): return GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123).split( data, groups=data["site_id"]) def pipeline(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical)], verbose_feature_names_out=False) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults def forest(): return pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)) # scikit-learn has no quantile forest, so gradient boosting with the quantile # loss gives the 5% and 95% points def quantile_ends(data): return [pipeline(GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", alpha=q, random_state=123)) .fit(data[predictors], data["abundance"]) for q in (0.05, 0.95)] ``` ::: ::: ### The Methods and Results paragraphs are written from the code On each fold the forest is fitted to nine tenths of the sites. On the tenth it gives its RMSE beside the average's, the share of catches inside its 90% intervals, and the rise in RMSE when each input is shuffled. It also gives mud's effect: its average prediction with every fitting station set to mud, over that with every station set to sand. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the rise in held-out RMSE when an input is shuffled, as in Feature importance shuffle_importance <- function(fitted, data, repeats = 10) { error <- \(d) rmse_vec(d$abundance, predict(fitted, d)$.pred) before <- error(data) columns <- setdiff(names(data), c("site_id", "abundance")) map(columns, \(input) { rises <- map_dbl(seq_len(repeats), \(i) { shuffled <- data shuffled[[input]] <- sample(shuffled[[input]]) error(shuffled) - before }) tibble(input, rise = mean(rises)) }) |> list_rbind() } # the average prediction with every station set to one level, over that with # every station set to another level_ratio <- function(fitted, data, input, level, reference) { at <- function(value) { set <- data set[[input]] <- factor(value, levels = levels(data[[input]])) mean(predict(fitted, set)$.pred) } at(level) / at(reference) } on_fold <- function(split) { fitting <- training(split) held <- testing(split) fitted <- fit(forest, fitting) ends <- predict(extract_fit_engine(fitted), bake(extract_recipe(fitted), new_data = held), type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95))$predictions caught <- held$abundance list( score = tibble( forest_rmse = rmse_vec(caught, predict(fitted, held)$.pred), average_rmse = rmse_vec(caught, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(held))), coverage = mean(caught >= ends[, 1] & caught <= ends[, 2]), width = mean(ends[, 2] - ends[, 1]), mud = level_ratio(fitted, fitting, "substrate", "mud", "sand")), importance = shuffle_importance(fitted, held)) } report <- function(data) { folds <- map(site_folds(data)$splits, on_fold) list(scores = map(folds, "score") |> list_rbind(), importance = map(folds, "importance") |> list_rbind(names_to = "fold") |> mutate(random_top = max(rise[str_starts(input, "random")]), .by = fold)) } # folds_better comes first, before forest_rmse becomes the mean summary_of <- function(result) { result$scores |> summarise(folds_better = sum(forest_rmse < average_rmse), forest_rmse = mean(forest_rmse), average_rmse = mean(average_rmse), coverage = mean(coverage), width = mean(width), mud_low = min(mud), mud_high = max(mud)) } recorded <- report(modelling) summary_of(recorded) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| folds_better| forest_rmse| average_rmse| coverage| width| mud_low| mud_high| |------------:|-----------:|------------:|--------:|-----:|-------:|--------:| | 9| 4.41| 4.62| 0.95| 11.78| 1.1| 1.16|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # the rise in held-out RMSE when an input is shuffled, as in Feature importance def shuffle_importance(fitted, data, repeats=10): result = permutation_importance( fitted, data[predictors], data["abundance"], n_repeats=repeats, random_state=123, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") return pd.DataFrame({"input": predictors, "rise": result.importances_mean}) # the average prediction with every station set to one level, over that with # every station set to another def level_ratio(fitted, data, column, level, reference): def at(value): return fitted.predict(data[predictors].assign(**{column: value})).mean() return at(level) / at(reference) def report(data): scores, importance = [], [] for number, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(site_folds(data), start=1): fitting, held = data.iloc[fit_rows], data.iloc[held_rows] fitted = forest().fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) low, high = (end.predict(held[predictors]) for end in quantile_ends(fitting)) caught = held["abundance"].to_numpy() scores.append({ "forest_rmse": root_mean_squared_error( caught, fitted.predict(held[predictors])), "average_rmse": root_mean_squared_error( caught, np.full(len(held), fitting["abundance"].mean())), "coverage": np.mean((caught >= low) & (caught <= high)), "width": np.mean(high - low), "mud": level_ratio(fitted, fitting, "substrate", "mud", "sand")}) rises = shuffle_importance(fitted, held) random = rises["input"].str.startswith("random") importance.append(rises.assign( fold=number, random_top=rises.loc[random, "rise"].max())) return pd.DataFrame(scores), pd.concat(importance, ignore_index=True) def summary_of(result): scores, _ = result return pd.DataFrame([{ "folds_better": (scores["forest_rmse"] < scores["average_rmse"]).sum(), "forest_rmse": scores["forest_rmse"].mean(), "average_rmse": scores["average_rmse"].mean(), "coverage": scores["coverage"].mean(), "width": scores["width"].mean(), "mud_low": scores["mud"].min(), "mud_high": scores["mud"].max()}]) recorded = report(survey) summary_of(recorded).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | folds_better | forest_rmse | average_rmse | coverage | width | mud_low | mud_high | |---------------:|--------------:|---------------:|-----------:|--------:|----------:|-----------:| | 10 | 4.28 | 4.71 | 0.94 | 11.46 | 1.13 | 1.2 | ::: ::: ::: On each fold an input either beats all three random columns or it does not, and the count of folds it beats them on says how far its score is more than chance. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beats_of <- function(result) { result$importance |> filter(!str_starts(input, "random")) |> summarise(folds_above_random = sum(rise > random_top), median_rise = median(rise), .by = input) |> arrange(desc(median_rise)) } beats <- beats_of(recorded) beats |> mutate(median_rise = round(median_rise, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|input | folds_above_random| median_rise| |:-----------------|------------------:|-----------:| |temperature_c | 10| 0.266| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 7| 0.117| |substrate | 6| 0.055| |depth_m | 6| 0.035| |season | 5| 0.030| |salinity_psu | 1| -0.016|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def beats_of(result): _, importance = result real = importance[~importance["input"].str.startswith("random")] return (real.assign(above=real["rise"] > real["random_top"]) .groupby("input") .agg(folds_above_random=("above", "sum"), median_rise=("rise", "median")) .sort_values("median_rise", ascending=False) .round(3) .reset_index()) beats_of(recorded) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | input | folds_above_random | median_rise | |:------------------|---------------------:|--------------:| | temperature_c | 10 | 0.2 | | depth_m | 8 | 0.098 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 7 | 0.082 | | season | 9 | 0.07 | | substrate | 5 | 0.044 | | salinity_psu | 2 | -0.011 | ::: ::: ::: The shapes come from a forest fitted to every station: its partial dependence over the middle 90% of each input, relative to its peak. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} everything <- fit(forest, modelling) # every station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 values, # averaged, relative to the highest shape_of <- function(input) { ends <- quantile(modelling[[input]], c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) value <- seq(ends[1], ends[2], length.out = 40) average <- map_dbl(value, \(level) { swept <- modelling swept[[input]] <- level mean(predict(everything, swept)$.pred) }) tibble(value, relative = average / max(average)) } shapes <- map(c(depth_m = "depth_m", temperature_c = "temperature_c"), shape_of) map(shapes, \(s) s |> slice(c(1, which.max(s$relative), n()))) |> list_rbind(names_to = "input") |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|input | value| relative| |:-------------|------:|--------:| |depth_m | 26.45| 0.99| |depth_m | 36.49| 1.00| |depth_m | 156.91| 0.61| |temperature_c | 4.14| 0.54| |temperature_c | 7.74| 1.00| |temperature_c | 13.50| 0.62|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} everything = forest().fit(survey[predictors], survey["abundance"]) # every station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 values, # averaged, relative to the highest def shape_of(column): result = partial_dependence(everything, survey[predictors], [column], percentiles=(0.05, 0.95), grid_resolution=40) average = result["average"][0] return pd.DataFrame({"value": result["grid_values"][0], "relative": average / average.max()}) shapes = {column: shape_of(column) for column in ["depth_m", "temperature_c"]} ends_and_peak = [shape.iloc[[0, shape["relative"].idxmax(), -1]].assign(input=column) for column, shape in shapes.items()] pd.concat(ends_and_peak, ignore_index=True)[["input", "value", "relative"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | input | value | relative | |:--------------|--------:|-----------:| | depth_m | 25.91 | 0.99 | | depth_m | 36 | 1 | | depth_m | 157.02 | 0.64 | | temperature_c | 4.13 | 0.58 | | temperature_c | 8.8 | 1 | | temperature_c | 13.71 | 0.72 | ::: ::: ::: Every number below comes from the code above, so the paragraphs change with the analysis and cannot drift from it. > **Methods.** We modelled the count of the species at 800 stations from > 160 sites with a random forest of 300 trees, fitted with > ranger 0.18.0 in R 4.6.1. The inputs were depth, > temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, substrate and season, and missing readings were > filled with the median of the stations used to fit. The forest was scored by > ten-fold cross-validation with whole sites held out, against predicting the average > on the same folds, drawn with seed 123. On each fold, each input was shuffled 10 > times on the held-out sites and its importance was the average rise in RMSE, > compared with three columns of random numbers added to the inputs. The 90% intervals > for single catches are the 5% and 95% points of a quantile forest, checked on the > held-out sites. Shapes are partial dependence from the forest fitted to every > station, and the effect of mud is the ratio of each fold's average prediction with > every station set to mud and to sand. The data, the code and the package versions > are archived with the paper. > **Results.** On held-out sites the forest's RMSE was > 4.41 animals, against > 4.62 for predicting the average (5% > lower), and it was lower on 9 of the 10 folds. > Shuffling temperature, chlorophyll, substrate and depth raised the error by more than any column of random > numbers on most folds (10, 7, 6 and 6 of 10); shuffling > season and salinity did not. The count peaked in cool water, near > 7.7 °C, and fell to 54% of > the peak at 4.1 °C and to > 62% at 13.5 °C. At the > same other inputs, muddy stations held between 1.10 and 1.16 times as many animals > as sandy ones across the ten fold models. The 90% intervals for single catches were > on average 11.8 animals wide and held > 95% of the held-out catches. Depth follows distance > offshore on this survey, so although the forest relied on it, its curve is not read > as a response to depth. The Methods paragraph gives what a reader needs to re-run the report, and the baseline the score is judged against. The Results paragraph puts the score beside that baseline and names only the inputs that beat the random columns on most folds. It gives temperature's effect as a shape with its range, and the interval with the coverage it reached. Mud's effect comes with its spread across the fold models, which is not a confidence interval: the fold models share nine tenths of their sites, so they agree more than models fitted to separate surveys would. ### The simulation confirms the temperature shape but not a depth peak No real study can check its shapes against the truth. The survey is simulated, so the forest's shapes can be checked against the ones the simulation used, as in [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the curves the simulation used, on the log scale, and where they peak true_curve <- list( depth_m = \(depth) -0.55 * ((depth - 80) / 60)^2, temperature_c = \(temperature) -0.60 * ((temperature - 9) / 3)^2 ) true_peak <- c(depth_m = 80, temperature_c = 9) checked <- imap(shapes, \(shape, input) { peak <- shape$value[which.max(shape$relative)] nearest <- which.min(abs(shape$value - true_peak[[input]])) tibble(forest_peak = peak, simulation_peak = true_peak[[input]], simulation_at_forest_peak = exp(true_curve[[input]](peak)), forest_at_simulation_peak = shape$relative[nearest]) }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "input") checked |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|input | forest_peak| simulation_peak| simulation_at_forest_peak| forest_at_simulation_peak| |:-------------|-----------:|---------------:|-------------------------:|-------------------------:| |depth_m | 36.49| 80| 0.75| 0.72| |temperature_c | 7.74| 9| 0.90| 0.98|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # the curves the simulation used, on the log scale, and where they peak true_curve = { "depth_m": lambda depth: -0.55 * ((depth - 80) / 60) ** 2, "temperature_c": lambda temperature: -0.60 * ((temperature - 9) / 3) ** 2, } true_peak = {"depth_m": 80, "temperature_c": 9} rows = [] for column, shape in shapes.items(): peak = shape["value"][shape["relative"].idxmax()] nearest = (shape["value"] - true_peak[column]).abs().idxmin() rows.append({"input": column, "forest_peak": peak, "simulation_peak": true_peak[column], "simulation_at_forest_peak": np.exp(true_curve[column](peak)), "forest_at_simulation_peak": shape["relative"][nearest]}) pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | input | forest_peak | simulation_peak | simulation_at_forest_peak | forest_at_simulation_peak | |:--------------|--------------:|------------------:|----------------------------:|----------------------------:| | depth_m | 36 | 80 | 0.74 | 0.75 | | temperature_c | 8.8 | 9 | 1 | 0.99 | ::: ::: ::: The temperature sentence holds. The forest's shape peaks at 7.7 °C and the simulation's at 9 °C; at the forest's peak the simulation's curve stands at 90% of its own peak. The shape, a hump in cool water, is right. An optimum quoted as 7.7 °C would be 1.3 °C out, which is why the paragraph gives the shape and its range rather than an optimum. The mud sentence holds in direction. The simulation gave muddy stations 1.49 times as many animals as sandy ones, more than any fold model found. Many of a forest's leaves hold stations of several substrates, and averaging over them pulls the difference towards nothing, so the direction is a safer claim than the size. The depth curve does not hold. The forest's peaks at 36 m and the simulation's at 80 m, where the forest's has fallen to 72% of its peak. Deep stations are also far offshore, and [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) found that no model separates the two on this survey. The Results paragraph declined to read the depth curve, and the check shows that was right. The survey cannot support three other sentences that are often written: - **"Salinity has no effect."** Salinity beat the random columns on only 1 of the 10 folds, which says the survey shows no sign of an effect, not that there is none. A small effect would fail the same way. - **"Warming will reduce the count."** The model describes how the count varies across the stations sampled. Water warmer than any station is outside them, as [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) showed, and [Communicating uncertainty](communicating-uncertainty.qmd) found an interval that lost its coverage at stations unlike those that set it. - **"Temperature drives the count."** Every shape here describes how the count varies with the inputs as they were found together. A cause needs an experiment or knowledge of the species. ### A gear that misses animals on mud reverses a finding and improves the score Grabs and dredges catch different shares of the animals on different ground. Suppose the survey's gear kept each animal on mud with a chance of one half, and every other animal. The records on mud would be halved, with nothing else changed, and the whole report is run again on the same folds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(77) # on mud the gear keeps each animal with a chance of one half biased <- modelling |> mutate(abundance = if_else(substrate == "mud", rbinom(n(), abundance, 0.5), abundance)) missed <- report(biased) bind_rows("As recorded" = summary_of(recorded), "Half missed on mud" = summary_of(missed), .id = "records") |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|records | folds_better| forest_rmse| average_rmse| coverage| width| mud_low| mud_high| |:------------------|------------:|-----------:|------------:|--------:|-----:|-------:|--------:| |As recorded | 9| 4.41| 4.62| 0.95| 11.78| 1.1| 1.16| |Half missed on mud | 9| 3.86| 4.03| 0.95| 9.87| 0.9| 0.95|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(77) # on mud the gear keeps each animal with a chance of one half biased = survey.copy() on_mud = biased["substrate"] == "mud" biased.loc[on_mud, "abundance"] = rng.binomial( biased.loc[on_mud, "abundance"].to_numpy(), 0.5) missed = report(biased) pd.concat([summary_of(recorded), summary_of(missed)], keys=["As recorded", "Half missed on mud"]).droplevel(1).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | folds_better | forest_rmse | average_rmse | coverage | width | mud_low | mud_high | |:-------------------|---------------:|--------------:|---------------:|-----------:|--------:|----------:|-----------:| | As recorded | 10 | 4.28 | 4.71 | 0.94 | 11.46 | 1.13 | 1.2 | | Half missed on mud | 9 | 3.73 | 4.1 | 0.93 | 9.17 | 0.79 | 0.85 | ::: ::: ::: As recorded, every fold model put mud above sand, between 1.10 and 1.16 times as many animals. With half the animals on mud missed, every one put it below, between 0.90 and 0.95, and the Results paragraph would now say that muddy stations hold fewer animals than sandy ones. The change is the gear's, not the species'. The score did not warn of it. The forest's RMSE fell from 4.41 to 3.86, it still beat the average on 9 of the 10 folds, and its intervals held 95% of the held-out catches. Cross-validation compares the model with the records, and every fold carries the same bias: the held-out sites lose the same half on mud as the sites used to fit. The smaller counts on mud are also easier to predict, so the error fell. Checks on the records come from outside the model: - **Comparing gears.** Fishing the same ground with two gears, or with a gear of known catch, measures how much each misses on each kind of ground. - **An independent method.** Video, acoustics or divers count the animals another way, and a model that agrees with them on mud has not learned the gear. - **Reporting the gear and the effort.** A reader who knows how the animals were caught can judge how far the records match the water. [Exploring and cleaning the data](../02-marine-data/exploring-and-cleaning.qmd) compared records by group, such as vessel or gear, and so finds a gear that differs from the rest. A bias shared by every haul shows up only against one of the checks above. ## A claim reports a finding with its certainty and reach The two paragraphs on this page follow from the whole course. The score is given beside a baseline, on sites the model never saw. Only inputs that beat random numbers again and again are named. The effects are given as shapes and ratios with their spread, and the intervals with the coverage they reached. Sentences the design cannot support, such as the depth peak, are left out with the reason. The report of [Reproducibility and transparent reporting](reproducibility.qmd) lets a reader re-run all of it, and the gear and effort let a reader judge how far the records match the water. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **claim** says what was found, how sure the finding is, and how far it reaches. The Methods paragraph says what was done and what the score is judged against; the Results paragraph gives the score beside its baseline and each effect with its spread. - Written from the code with inline numbers, the paragraphs cannot drift from the analysis: here the forest's RMSE was 4.41 against 4.62 for the average, and its 90% intervals held 95% of held-out catches. - The simulation confirmed the temperature shape, a hump in cool water, and mud's direction but not its size. It did not confirm a depth peak: depth follows distance offshore, and no model separates the two on this survey. - A gear that missed half the animals on mud turned more animals on mud into fewer, in every fold model, and the cross-validated error fell. Validation compares a model with the records, not the records with the water. - Checks on the records come from outside the model: comparing gears, an independent method, and reporting the gear and the effort. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Make the gear miss half the animals on rock instead of mud. Rock has only 55 stations. How do rock's ratio to sand and the cross-validated score change, and would the report have caught it? 2.
